note: Navigation-accuracy baseline (#328). Regenerate with `UPDATE_PERF_BASELINE=1 cargo test -p strapdown-core --test perf_baseline`, then review the diff: every changed number is a claim about the navigation solution. Values are rounded to 6 significant figures. `null` means the metric is not computable for that scenario -- dead reckoning reports no covariance -- and is not gated. `"gated": false` keeps a metric recorded but unasserted. See the module docs in core/tests/perf_baseline.rs for what the numbers do and do not measure.

real_clean__ekf.description: test_data.csv, GNSS every epoch, no fault

containment_3sigma_horizontal.note: 0.494, down from an unfalsifiable 1.000; see the UKF row. The EKF applied the absolute floor in both predict and update, so its fabricated sigma was 493 m.

npes_position.note: Not the horizontal channel: containment reads a flat 1.000 there, so each horizontal term is bounded by 9. Almost all of this is the vertical channel, whose containment is 0.41. The EKF here is over-conservative horizontally (see core/tests/aiding.rs, `a_note_on_filter_consistency`) and over-confident vertically at the same time. Recorded as measured, not as a target.

npes_position.note: Horizontally over-confident, unlike the UKF and EKF rows: containment is 0.16 here against their 1.000. containment_3sigma_horizontal.note: 0.526, down from an unfalsifiable 1.000. Before #373 this filter reported a horizontal sigma floored at 201 m against an actual error of metres, so its error could not leave the band. The remaining gap to 0.9973 is genuine over-confidence and is what #373's acceptance criterion 2 asks to be characterised -- a real number to work on rather than a constant.

npes_position.note: 4,986, up from 347. The denominator is no longer inflated by #373's 201 m floor, so this now reports the covariance the filter actually holds under an AR(1) position fault. High and honest; #372 and #373 own closing it.

real_outage_60s__eskf.description: test_data.csv, 120 s of GNSS then a 60 s outage, repeating

horizontal_max_m.note: A single-sample statistic at the end of a 60 s free-inertial coast, so it swings more than the RMS beside it.

nees_position.note: 83.04 against `npes_position`'s 73.43, a ratio of 1.13 -- the largest honest gap between the two in the matrix. This is what #376 was for: the diagonal-only form assumes the position states are uncorrelated, and during a 60 s free-inertial coast they are not. Error accumulates along a correlated direction with no fix to break it up, so the diagonal form understates the inconsistency by 13% here. Everywhere the filter is being aided every epoch the two agree to 1%.

real_rbpf_slice__rbpf.description: first 1200 records of test_data.csv, GNSS every epoch, 500 particles

horizontal_cep95_m.note: Not gated: this row's tail statistics are platform-dependent, because the tail IS the handful of epochs where the particle cloud collapses (#385). Measured on the same commit, Linux 34.02 m against Windows 24.33 m -- a 28.5% spread, wider than the improve band, so a Linux bless fails the Windows leg. The bulk statistics on this row agree across platforms to about 1% (horizontal_rmse_m +1.3%, containment_3sigma_horizontal +0.8%) and stay gated. horizontal_max_m is the same kind of statistic and currently sits at +4.7%, inside the band; it is worth watching rather than pre-emptively ungating. Re-gate this when #385 lands. Note also that the baseline is blessed on one platform and gated on three, with no cross-platform tolerance anywhere in judge() -- see #386.

nees_position.note: Not gated, for the same reason as `npes_position` on this row: both are dominated by the RBPF covariance collapse (#385), not by navigation accuracy. 17 of 1,200 epochs report a horizontal sigma of nanometres, and a mean of a ratio cannot survive a near-zero denominator. Note the real NEES reads 2.4e14 against the diagonal form's 5.7e25 -- eleven orders apart, both meaningless. Re-gate when #385 lands.

npes_position.note: Not gated: dominated by an RBPF covariance collapse, not by navigation accuracy. 17 of 1,200 epochs report a horizontal sigma below 1 mm -- the smallest is 4.2 nm -- so this mean of e^2/P is set by a near-zero denominator on ~1.4% of rows. Exposed rather than caused by #367: before it, every row was sampled one IMU step late, after `predict` had re-inflated the cloud, which hid the collapse and recorded 183.5 here. Tracked in #385. `containment_3sigma_horizontal` on this row is unaffected and stays gated.

syn_cruise_1hz__ekf.description: synthetic 300 s at 50 Hz, GNSS every 1 s, scored against exact truth

containment_3sigma_vertical.note: Down under #375. With the barometer scheduled at 1 Hz instead of firing on all fifty records a second, the vertical error is larger and carries a systematic bias the filter does not model, so the 3-sigma envelope no longer covers it. The horizontal containment on the same row is unchanged. This is the #372 measurement, taken without the 50 Hz aiding that used to hide it.

npes_position.note: Up under #375, entirely through the vertical channel: the horizontal columns on this row moved by less than half a percent, while `vertical_rmse_m` went ~0.5 to ~2.2-2.8 m and `vertical_bias_m` from about zero to -0.6 to -2.0 m. A normalised error takes that unmodelled bias into a covariance that did not grow to meet it. The gap is #372's to close; the 50 Hz barometer was masking it.

vertical_bias_m.note: About zero before #375 and -0.6 to -2.0 m after it. This is the number that makes the case for #372's barometer bias state: at 50 Hz the aid was strong enough to crush a systematic altitude offset, and at the 1 Hz a real barometer logs at, it is what the vertical channel actually does. Nothing here models it.

vertical_rmse_m.note: Roughly 4x worse than at a 50 Hz barometer, and the honest price of #375 scheduling it. `generate_synthetic` fills `relative_altitude` on every record, so before #375 this 50 Hz scenario received fifty pressure readings a second, each entering as an independent fix; averaging fifty samples cuts the effective noise about sevenfold and pinned altitude to the truth. At the 1 Hz the reference recording actually logs, it does not. Note `vertical_bias_m` on the same row moved from about zero to -0.6 to -2.0 m: what is left is a systematic offset, not noise, and an unmodelled offset under a tight R is exactly #372. The real-data rows did not move at all -- they were already 1 Hz.

yaw_rmse_deg.note: 108.3 deg, from 96.6 before #375 and 42.7 before #373 -- and this row still has no magnetometer, so yaw is observable only through the GNSS velocity fix. The EKF reaches 0.97 deg on the identical stream. Not a tuning loss and not this change's doing: an alpha sweep at 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 0.5 and 1.0 reads 89.8, 90.5, 90.1, 96.5 and 108.3 deg, so widening the sigma-point spread makes it worse and the tiny `n + lambda` scaling is NOT the cause. That refutes the conditioning hypothesis and leaves #371's original diagnosis, the linear Euler mean over sigma-point attitudes, as the live one. Uniformly random yaw is about 104 deg RMS, so this filter has no heading at all.

npes_position.note: `sim::dead_reckoning` emits no covariance, so the three consistency metrics are `null` here. This scenario is what exercises that path end to end.

syn_outage_60s__eskf.description: synthetic 300 s at 50 Hz, 60 s of GNSS then 60 s of outage

horizontal_max_m.note: As `real_outage_60s__eskf`: a single sample at the end of a coast.

horizontal_rmse_m.note: Worse under #375, which is the same vertical story as the `syn_cruise_1hz` rows and, on this scenario, a compounding one: through a 60 s GNSS outage the barometer is the only aiding source there is, so dropping it from 50 Hz to 1 Hz removes almost all of it. Roll and pitch degrade with it, and horizontal dead reckoning follows the attitude. 24 m of horizontal error over a 60 s free-inertial coast on consumer-grade IMU is a realistic figure; the 12 m it replaces was flattered by a barometer no hardware runs at.

horizontal_cep95_m.note: 650 m, down from 3,152. See `horizontal_rmse_m` on this row: scheduling the barometer at 1 Hz took the whole distribution down, not just its centre.

horizontal_max_m.note: As `real_outage_60s__eskf`: a single sample at the end of a coast.

horizontal_rmse_m.note: 235 m, down from 858 -- the largest single improvement in this bless, and the reason #375 had to land before #369. A 50 Hz barometer through a 60 s free-inertial coast was actively destabilising this filter: `horizontal_cep95_m` fell 3,152 to 650 m, `horizontal_max_m` 3,757 to 1,498 m, `nees_position` 18.45 to 6.82 and `containment_3sigma_horizontal` 0.912 to 0.989 against an ideal of 0.9973, all on the same change. Still far worse than the ESKF's equivalent row, which is #371.

nees_position.note: 6.82 against `npes_position`'s 6.54, a ratio of 1.04 -- down from 1.22 before #375, when this was the largest gap in the matrix. A free-inertial coast correlates the position error and the diagonal-only form cannot see it; with the coast better controlled there is less correlation for it to miss.
